title: Where did the first living cell come from?
realQuestion:
Everything alive descends from something alive. Run that backwards far enough and you reach a first thing that did not, and nobody knows how it started.

That much is agreed. What is disputed is what the gap means. One side says the difficulty is not ordinary: a cell runs on a coded sequence, and we have never once seen a code written by anything but a mind. The other side says the gap is the ordinary shape of an unsolved problem in a young field, that it has been narrowing steadily for seventy years, and that 'we cannot yet do it' has never been a reason to conclude 'it cannot be done'.

This is not the argument about evolution. Evolution starts once something can copy itself imperfectly; how the first copier arose is a separate question ([[abiogenesis]]), and Darwin's theory does not answer it and was never meant to.

distinctions.label: Does evolution depend on solving this?
distinctions.gloss: No, and both sides here agree. Natural selection needs a population that already replicates. Common descent rests on evidence that stands whatever the answer to this page turns out to be. Set aside, and argued in topic 6.

distinctions.label: Is there a demonstrated route from chemistry to a living cell?
distinctions.gloss: Not yet, and everyone says so. The disagreement is about what follows from that — whether it is a gap of the kind that gets closed, or a gap of a kind that does not. This is the argument on this page.

distinctions.label: Would a designer have to be God?
distinctions.gloss: A further step the design inference does not take by itself. Getting from 'a mind' to anything worth worshipping needs the arguments in topics 2 and 5. Not attempted here.

glossary.definition: The origin of life from non-living chemistry. A separate question from evolution, which explains what happens after something can already reproduce.
The proposal that RNA came before both DNA and proteins, because RNA can both carry information and act as a catalyst. Widely held, not established, and not the only candidate.

In this argument, a sequence that is both improbable and does a particular job — as a sentence is, and a random string of the same length is not. Whether the term names one thing or two is part of the dispute.
A difference in acidity across a membrane. Every living cell uses one to make energy, which is why finding a natural one in the right place matters to this argument.
A membrane-bounded droplet that grows and divides without being alive. Made in laboratories; the gap between one of these and a cell is the gap this page is about.

sides.label: A code is the kind of thing that needs an author

arguments.claim: Every code we know the history of was written by someone, and the cell runs on a code
arguments.explanation:
The argument is not that the origin of life is hard. It is that the thing needing explanation is of a particular kind. DNA does not merely have structure, like a crystal; it carries a sequence that specifies something else, in a mapping that is arbitrary in the way an alphabet is arbitrary — nothing about the chemistry of the three-letter group CAG makes it mean glutamine.

Stephen Meyer's case is an inference from experience rather than from ignorance: wherever we can trace a [[specified information]] sequence to its source, the source turns out to be a mind. Applying that to the one case where we cannot watch is, he argues, the ordinary way historical sciences reason, not a departure from it.

quote.text: Our uniform experience affirms that specified or functional information—whether inscribed in hieroglyphics, written in a book, encoded in a radio signal, or produced in an RNA-world 'ribozyme-engineering' experiment—always arises from an intelligent source, from a mind, not a strictly material process.
quote.author: Stephen C. Meyer
quote.locator: the design inference as Meyer states it; the same argument runs through Signature in the Cell (2009)

counter.objection: The premise is doing all the work and it is the disputed one. 'Uniform experience' of coded information is uniform experience of human artefacts, and of nothing else — the sample is one species over a few thousand years. Extending it to a case four billion years old, in conditions nobody has observed, is not induction but assumption. And the arbitrariness of the genetic code is itself under investigation: several of its assignments track the chemistry of the amino acids they name, which is what you would expect if the mapping grew rather than being assigned.
counter.response: That a sample is limited is a reason for caution, not a reason to prefer the alternative, which has no positive instances at all. Nobody has watched unguided chemistry write a code either.

variants.label: Evolutionary creation
variants.heldBy: Francis Collins and BioLogos; Denis Alexander; the mainstream position in Catholic and Anglican theology
variants.oneLine: God is the author of the whole process, including whatever chemistry produced the first cell — so the origin of life is a scientific problem, not evidence for him.
variants.summary:
This position holds everything the design inference holds about God and almost nothing it holds about method. Creation is not a series of interventions but the existence and lawfulness of the whole system, so a natural route from chemistry to life would not be a defeat for theism; it would be a description of how God did it.

Collins is explicit that the opposite strategy is dangerous, and he applies the warning to intelligent design by name. Faith attached to a currently unsolved problem inherits that problem's fate.

quote.text: Faith that places God in the gaps of current understanding about the natural world may be headed for crisis if advances in science subsequently fill those gaps.
quote.author: Francis S. Collins
quote.work: The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above cannot start, because this position makes no inference from information to a designer. Telling it that our uniform experience of codes is uniform experience of human artefacts is telling it something it already grants and has no use for: it is not arguing from the code at all.

objection.text: If God acts entirely through natural causes at the origin of life, then nothing about the origin of life is evidence of him, and the position is empirically indistinguishable from the naturalism it is contrasted with. Intelligent design proponents press this as an abdication; atheists press it as a concession. Both are asking the same question — what work is God doing here that could ever be noticed?
objection.response: Indistinguishable within chemistry, which is the only place the comparison is being run. The claim was never that God is one cause among the chemical ones, and a doctrine of creation that required him to be would be the weaker one.

variants.label: Direct creation, recently
variants.heldBy: Answers in Genesis; Ken Ham; the Institute for Creation Research
variants.oneLine: Life did not arise from chemistry at all: living kinds were made directly, within the last ten thousand years, and the law of biogenesis says so.
variants.summary:
The strongest form of the theist side, and the one that concedes least. It does not argue that a designer is the best explanation of a chemical difficulty; it denies there was a chemical episode to explain. The scientific argument offered is the law of biogenesis — that life has never been observed to come from non-life — treated not as a summary of current experience but as a standing law with a named author.

It is set out here at its own strength rather than through a critic, and its constituency is large: this is what a substantial minority of American Christians are taught.

quote.text: Life only comes from life. This was the law established by the Author of Life, Who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life—Jesus Christ.
quote.author: Answers in Genesis

variants.againstSettledCore: This conflicts with the settled core of topic 6, which is not a matter of dispute among biologists and geologists: living species descend with modification from shared ancestors, and the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. The dating is established independently by radiometric methods, ice cores, varves, coral growth bands and starlight travel time, and no result in any of those fields supports a recent creation. The position is printed here at full strength because it is genuinely held and because paraphrasing it through its critics would be the mistake this site was built to avoid — and marked because printing it unmarked would be the other one.
variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above is aimed at an inference this position does not make. It is not reasoning from the improbability of a sequence to a mind; it is denying that any prebiotic sequence occurred, on the authority of a text. An argument about the limits of induction from human artefacts has nothing to engage.

objection.text: The law of biogenesis is a generalisation from observation, not a law with modal force, and it is being asked to do work no empirical generalisation can do: rule out an event nobody was present for. Old-earth and evolutionary creationists object on the same ground as geologists — that the position requires the independent dating methods to be wrong in a coordinated way nobody has explained — and add a theological objection, that hanging the faith on a claim the evidence contradicts sets a young believer up to lose both at once.
objection.response: The dating methods rest on assumptions about initial conditions and constant rates that cannot themselves be observed, and Scripture is a better-attested witness to origins than an extrapolation is.

arguments.claim: The space of possible sequences is far too large for an undirected search to have found a working one
arguments.explanation:
This is the empirical claim the inference rests on, and it is a number rather than an intuition. Douglas Axe, working on a fragment of a β-lactamase enzyme, estimated how much of sequence space produces a chain that folds into a working active site at all.

If functional sequences are that rare, then the question is not whether a blind search is slow but whether it is possible: there have not been enough seconds, enough molecules or enough planets. The argument concludes that the search must have been directed, because nothing else could have found the target.

quote.text: of the possible genes encoding protein chains 153 amino acids in length, only about one in a hundred trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion is expected to encode a chain that folds well enough to perform a biological function!
quote.author: Douglas Axe
quote.work: Undeniable: How Biology Confirms Our Intuition That Life Is Designed
quote.locator: the popular statement of the estimate published in the Journal of Molecular Biology, 2004

counter.objection: The estimate measures one fold in one protein and then treats functional sequences as isolated islands in a space that has to be searched blind. Both assumptions are contested by protein evolution researchers: functional regions may be connected rather than isolated, the search is not blind because selection retains partial success, and a count of sequences that produce one specific fold is not a count of sequences that would have done some job. A separate objection, pressed by Christians at BioLogos and elsewhere, is strategic rather than technical: resting a case for God on a currently unsolved problem puts him where the ignorance is, so that every advance in prebiotic chemistry becomes a small defeat for faith.
counter.response: The inference is not from ignorance but from a positive claim about what minds do and what chemistry does not. And an argument that would be weakened by a discovery is in that respect an ordinary scientific argument, not a disreputable one.

sides.label: The chemistry is being worked out, step by step

arguments.claim: Alkaline vents supply, for free, the one thing every living cell runs on
arguments.explanation:
The strongest version of this side is not a promissory note. Every cell alive powers itself with a [[proton gradient]] across a membrane — a fact so universal it almost certainly predates the split between bacteria and archaea, and so strange that it needs explaining.

Alkaline hydrothermal vents produce exactly that gradient without any biology, in a labyrinth of thin mineral walls with catalytic iron-sulphur surfaces on them. On this account the puzzle inverts: life did not have to invent its energy system, it grew inside one that was already running.

quote.text: the difference in pH across thin barriers produced natural proton gradients with equivalent magnitude and polarity to the proton-motive force required for carbon fixation in extant bacteria and archaea
quote.author: Victor Sojo, Barry Herschy, Alexandra Whicher, Eloi Camprubí and Nick Lane
quote.work: The Origin of Life in Alkaline Hydrothermal Vents, Astrobiology 16(2)

counter.objection: A gradient is energy, and energy is not the problem. Ice on a hillside has a gradient. What has to be explained is a system that harnesses one to build and copy itself, and the distance between a mineral pore doing chemistry and a cell running a metabolism is exactly the distance in question. Naming a plausible location is not the same as demonstrating a route.
counter.response: It is not only a location. The claim is that the specific mechanism modern cells use is present in the environment before any cell exists, which is a testable prediction rather than a hope, and reactors built to test it have produced organic molecules from carbon dioxide and hydrogen.

variants.label: Replication first
variants.heldBy: John Sutherland, Matthew Powner; Jack Szostak; Gerald Joyce
variants.oneLine: What had to come first was a molecule that copies itself, and the chemistry for making its parts is being built step by step in the laboratory.
variants.summary:
The other half of the field, and it disagrees with the vent hypothesis about what the first thing was. On this account life begins when something starts copying itself with errors, because that is the point at which selection can start; metabolism follows.

The programme is synthetic rather than geological: rather than looking for a place where the chemistry could have happened, it works out routes by which the molecules could have been made, and it has dissolved objections that stood for decades. The standard complaint against the [[RNA world]] was that its building blocks could not be made — ribose is hard to form selectively, and joining a base to a sugar does not work for the pyrimidines RNA uses. Sutherland's group answered it by finding a route that never produces free ribose or a free base at all.

quote.text: activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides can be formed in a short sequence that bypasses free ribose and the nucleobases, and instead proceeds through arabinose amino-oxazoline and anhydronucleoside intermediates
quote.author: Matthew Powner, Béatrice Gerland and John Sutherland
quote.work: Synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides in prebiotically plausible conditions, Nature 459

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above is that a gradient is only energy, and that naming a plausible location is not demonstrating a route. This programme is not naming a location. It is building routes, in reagents and steps, and can be argued with on the chemistry rather than on the geology — which is a different conversation with different evidence in it.

objection.text: A chemist choosing reagents in a chosen order is doing what an unattended planet does not. Each synthesis is real, and each is also a demonstration that the step is possible under conditions someone selected, which is why the field's own name for the difficulty is the water problem and the concentration problem rather than the impossibility problem.
objection.response: The conditions in these syntheses are chosen to be ones an early Earth plausibly supplied — wet-dry cycles, ultraviolet light, cyanide chemistry from impacts — and arguing about whether they were available is arguing about geology, which is progress.

arguments.claim: The hardest problems are stated in the field’s own literature, in its own words, and worked on
arguments.explanation:
A field in denial does not publish its difficulties under the heading 'paradoxes'. Steven Benner's paper does exactly that, and the sharpest of them is not one an outsider raised.

Leave organic chemistry running with energy and it does not tend towards life. It tends towards tar: heterogeneous, intractable mixtures that go nowhere. That is a general result across an enormous amount of experimental work, and it is a problem for every route including the ones argued for above. Benner's argument is methodological — that the way to make progress on origins is to name the paradoxes precisely enough to design experiments against them — and the state of the field is that this is being done in print rather than managed in public.

quote.text: An enormous amount of empirical data have established, as a rule, that organic systems, given energy and left to themselves, devolve to give uselessly complex mixtures, 'asphalts'
quote.author: Steven A. Benner
quote.work: Paradoxes in the Origin of Life, Origins of Life and Evolution of Biospheres 44
quote.locator: the asphalt paradox, one of several the paper sets out

counter.objection: Naming a problem is not solving it, and the honesty is being offered as though it were progress. The asphalt paradox is precisely what the design argument predicts: undirected chemistry with energy in it produces mess, and the exceptions are the cases where a chemist supplied the direction. A field that has been candid about this for a decade and has not resolved it is evidence that the difficulty is structural rather than temporary.
counter.response: Structural difficulties get solved too, and the asphalt paradox already has candidate answers — mineral surfaces, wet-dry cycling, systems chemistry that selects rather than accumulates. Whether they work is an experimental question, which is the position a problem is in when it is being worked on rather than declared closed.

notes.heading: What Miller and Urey actually showed, and what they did not
notes.text:
The 1953 spark-discharge experiment is the most cited and most misread result in the field. It produced amino acids from a simple gas mixture, which was genuinely surprising and remains a real result: the building blocks are easy, and they turn up in meteorites too.

It did not produce life, was not claimed to, and used an atmosphere richer in hydrogen than the early Earth's is now thought to have been. Both sides overreach here. It is not evidence that the problem is nearly solved, and it is not a failed experiment: it settled that the monomers are cheap, and moved the difficulty to how they are sequenced, which is where the difficulty has stayed.

notes.heading: How little time there was
notes.text:
This constrains both sides, and neither likes it. The Earth was uninhabitably hot until roughly 4.4 billion years ago, and there is reasonable evidence of life by about 3.7. That leaves a window of a few hundred million years, which is short for an undirected search and is a real difficulty for the chemistry.

It is not a difficulty for common descent, which is dated by different evidence entirely, and it is not by itself an argument for design — 'less time than expected' bears on how the thing happened, not on whether it needed a mind.

whereItStands:
Nobody has made a cell, and no route from chemistry to one has been demonstrated end to end. Anyone telling you otherwise, in either direction, is ahead of the evidence.

The field has moved, though, and in a particular way: the problems that looked most impossible from outside — making the monomers, making nucleotides, making membranes that grow and divide into [[protocell]]s — have turned out to be the tractable ones. The problem that has not moved is sequence. Getting a specific arrangement that does something, rather than a mixture of everything, is where the difficulty has sat since the 1960s and where it sits now.

What is genuinely unresolved is what that pattern means. It is consistent with a hard problem being worked through in the usual way, and it is consistent with the difficulty being of a different kind from the ones already solved. No result currently distinguishes those two readings, which is why this is an argument and not a finding.
commonMistake:
Christians most often treat the current gap as though it were the argument's foundation, which makes the case hostage to the next paper. If the design inference is sound it should be statable as a claim about what codes are, not as a claim about what chemists have not yet done; stated the second way it shrinks every year whether or not it is true.

Atheists most often answer a question that was not asked. 'Evolution does not need abiogenesis' is correct and is a reply to a different argument. So is listing what has been synthesised, when the objection was about sequence rather than about parts. Both moves let the actual claim through untouched.

And both sides quietly use the same bad inference in opposite directions: that the difficulty of a problem tells you something about its solution. It does not. A problem can be hard because the answer is unusual, or hard because it is old and the traces are gone.
